steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Draft the introduction for our theory paper explaining why multimodal contrastive learning like CLIP is robust to distribution shift. Motivate the problem, state what we explain and how (comparison with supervised learning), describe the mechanisms we identify and the role of captions, and mention the experiments.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- OOD generalization is hard; spurious features; MMCL as a promising direction
- Evidence that CLIP's zero-shot classifier is more robust
- Gap: no explanation; our goal and comparison to supervised learning
- Two mechanisms behind robustness
- Role of caption richness
- Experiments

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - generalizing under distribution shift / across domains: long-standing challenge
  - models learn simple, domain-dependent spurious features instead of generalizable ones (cite x4)
  - MMCL: significant robustness in zero-shot image classification
  - vision + language encoders, contrastive loss aligns paired image/text, pushes apart unpaired (CLIP, ALIGN; cite each)
- Evidence (CLIP paper)
  - CLIP-trained models better OOD generalization (their Fig 13)
  - zero-shot classifiers: higher OOD accuracy than supervised classifiers with equivalent ID accuracy, incl. existing robust methods
  - advantage diminishes with any label supervision, e.g. linear probing on CLIP image encoder (Fig 14 of CLIP paper)
  - => zero-shot classifier more robust than anything trained with label supervision
- Gap and goal
  - no comprehensive understanding of why
  - theory so far only on MMCL in-distribution generalization (cite x2), not OOD robustness
  - we explain how CLIP / MMCL produce robust zero-shot classifier; contributions of MMCL loss and captions
  - compare to classifiers from supervised learning (SL), representative of non-zero-shot methods (end-to-end SL, linear probing on unsupervised/self-supervised representations)
- Mechanisms (MMCL loss + rich captions)
  - (1) intra-class contrasting of image-text pairs in same latent class -> learns generalizable high-variance features when annotated by text
    - SL prone to simple spurious features over higher-variance generalizable ones (cite)
    - cow example: diverse cows on green grass; SL learns grass, MMCL learns cow
  - (2) inter-class feature sharing -> learn info about a class that only exists/annotated in other classes
    - tree example: trees all have green leaves; wolf image has leafless tree in background; MMCL disassociates green leaf from tree
    - SL learns green leaves as part of 'tree', fails on trees without green leaves
  - together: robust representations, generalize to unseen domains
- Captions
  - vary caption richness; rich captions essential
  - extreme: captions are just labels -> no robustness gain
- Experiments
  - synthetic experiment; real datasets MSCOCO, Conceptual Captions, shifted ImageNet
  - confirm roles of MMCL loss and rich captions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Learning classifiers that generalize under distribution shifts and across different domains has been a challenge in machine learning for a long time. One key reason is that modern models are very susceptible to learning simple spurious features in the training data that depend on the domain, instead of features that are more complex but generalize. Recently Multimodal Contrastive Learning (MMCL) has shown significant robustness in zero-shot image classification. MMCL trains a vision encoder and a language encoder with a contrastive loss so that representations of paired images and text are aligned, and representations of images and texts from different pairs are pushed apart (e.g., CLIP, ALIGN).

The CLIP authors have shown that models trained with CLIP, which is an example of MMCL algorithms, have better Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization (see their Fig 13). In particular, the zero-shot classifiers trained with CLIP get higher OOD accuracy than classifiers that have the same In-Distribution (ID) accuracy but are trained with different supervised learning techniques, including existing robust methods. Interestingly, if any label supervision is introduced the advantage of CLIP goes away, for example when doing linear probing with labeled data on CLIP's image encoder (see Fig 14 of their paper). Both of these findings suggest that the zero-shot classifier from CLIP is more robust to distribution shifts than any classifier trained with label supervision.

However, there is no comprehensive understanding in the literature of why this happens. The existing theoretical studies only looked at the in-distribution generalization of MMCL, and did not explore its OOD-robustness. In this paper we want to explain how CLIP, and MMCL more broadly, produces a zero-shot classifier that is more robust, and to make clear what the MMCL loss and the image captions each contribute. We do this by comparing the zero-shot classifier learned by MMCL with classifiers learned with supervised learning. Supervised learning is arguably representative of all the other non-zero-shot ways of training a classifier, since supervised learning is basically involved in them (e.g., end-to-end supervised learning, and linear probing on representations learned by unsupervised/self-supervised algorithms).

- Mechanisms (MMCL loss + rich captions), at least two
  - (1) intra-class contrasting -> learn generalizable high-variance features when annotated by text; SL prefers simple spurious features
    - cow on green grass: SL learns grass, MMCL learns cow
  - (2) inter-class feature sharing -> info about a class that exists/annotated only in other classes
    - leafless tree in wolf image; MMCL disassociates green leaf from tree; SL fails on trees without green leaves
  - together: robust to distribution shift, generalize to unseen domains
- Captions: richness essential; captions = labels -> no gain
- Experiments: synthetic; MSCOCO, Conceptual Captions, shifted ImageNet; validate theory

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Learning classifiers that generalize under distribution shifts and across different domains has been a challenge in machine learning for a long time. One key reason is that modern models are very susceptible to learning simple spurious features in the training data that depend on the domain, instead of features that are more complex but generalize. Recently Multimodal Contrastive Learning (MMCL) has shown significant robustness in zero-shot image classification. MMCL trains a vision encoder and a language encoder with a contrastive loss so that representations of paired images and text are aligned, and representations of images and texts from different pairs are pushed apart (e.g., CLIP, ALIGN).

The CLIP authors have shown that models trained with CLIP, which is an example of MMCL algorithms, have better Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization (see their Fig 13). In particular, the zero-shot classifiers trained with CLIP get higher OOD accuracy than classifiers that have the same In-Distribution (ID) accuracy but are trained with different supervised learning techniques, including existing robust methods. Interestingly, if any label supervision is introduced the advantage of CLIP goes away, for example when doing linear probing with labeled data on CLIP's image encoder (see Fig 14 of their paper). Both of these findings suggest that the zero-shot classifier from CLIP is more robust to distribution shifts than any classifier trained with label supervision.

However, there is no comprehensive understanding in the literature of why this happens. The existing theoretical studies only looked at the in-distribution generalization of MMCL, and did not explore its OOD-robustness. In this paper we want to explain how CLIP, and MMCL more broadly, produces a zero-shot classifier that is more robust, and to make clear what the MMCL loss and the image captions each contribute. We do this by comparing the zero-shot classifier learned by MMCL with classifiers learned with supervised learning. Supervised learning is arguably representative of all the other non-zero-shot ways of training a classifier, since supervised learning is basically involved in them (e.g., end-to-end supervised learning, and linear probing on representations learned by unsupervised/self-supervised algorithms).

We show that the MMCL loss together with rich image captions enables at least two mechanisms that make zero-shot classification robust. (1) Contrasting image-text pairs within the same latent class (intra-class contrasting) lets MMCL easily learn generalizable features with a high variance, when they are annotated by text. SL on the other hand is very prone to learning simple spurious features instead of the more generalizable features with higher variance. For example, if most of the cow images, with diverse shapes and colors, are on a simple green grass background, SL learns the grass to predict 'cow', but MMCL successfully learns the cow. (2) The MMCL loss enables inter-class feature sharing, which allows learning information about a class that only exists and is annotated in other classes. For example, if all the images of the tree class have green leaves but an image in the wolf class has a tree without leaves in the background, MMCL can disassociate the green leaf from the tree class. SL cannot use this information and learns the green leaves as an indistinguishable part of 'tree'. So it fails to classify trees without green leaves in the test data. The two mechanisms together let MMCL learn representations that are robust to distribution shift and generalize to unseen domains.

We also want to show that captions are important, so we analyze what happens when the richness of captions varies, and we show that rich captions are essential to get robustness. In the extreme case where the captions are just labels, there is no gain in robustness.

We support the theoretical findings with experiments, a well-designed synthetic experiment and also experiments on real datasets, including MSCOCO, Conceptual Captions, and shifted versions of ImageNet. The results show that the MMCL loss function and rich captions play crucial roles in achieving robustness, which further validates the theoretical findings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Learning classifiers that generalize under distribution shifts and across various domains has long been a challenge in machine learning. A key reason is that modern models are highly susceptible to learning simple, domain-dependent spurious features in the training data instead of more complex but generalizable features [1,2,3,4]. Recently, Multimodal Contrastive Learning (MMCL) has demonstrated significant robustness in zero-shot image classification. It trains vision and language encoders with a contrastive loss to align the representations of paired images and text, while pushing apart the representations of images and texts from different pairs (e.g., CLIP [5], ALIGN [6]).

[5] have shown that models trained with CLIP, an example of MMCL algorithms, exhibit better Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization (c.f. their Fig 13). Specifically, CLIP-trained zero-shot classifiers achieve higher OOD accuracy than classifiers with equivalent In-Distribution (ID) accuracy that are trained with various supervised learning techniques, including existing robust methods. Interestingly, the advantage of CLIP diminishes if any label supervision is introduced, e.g., through linear probing with labeled data on CLIP's image encoder (c.f. Fig 14 of [5]). Both findings suggest that the zero-shot classifier produced by CLIP is more robust to distribution shifts than any classifier trained with label supervision.

However, a comprehensive understanding of the reasons behind this does not yet exist in the literature. Existing theoretical studies have only examined MMCL's in-distribution generalization [7,8], and have not explored its OOD-robustness. In this paper, we aim to explain how CLIP, and more broadly MMCL, produces a zero-shot classifier with superior robustness, while clarifying the contributions of the MMCL loss and the image captions. We do this by comparing the zero-shot classifier learned through MMCL with classifiers learned via supervised learning. The latter is arguably representative of all other non-zero-shot methods of classifier training, since supervised learning is essentially involved in them (e.g., end-to-end supervised learning, and linear probing on representations learned by unsupervised/self-supervised algorithms).

Specifically, we show that the MMCL loss accompanied by rich image captions enables at least two mechanisms that provide robustness to zero-shot classification. (1) The intra-class contrasting between image-text pairs within the same latent class enables MMCL to easily learn generalizable features with a high variance, when they are annotated by text. In contrast, SL is highly prone to learning simple spurious features instead of the more generalizable features with a higher variance [9]. For example, if the majority of cow images with diverse shapes and colors appear on a simple green grass background, SL learns the grass to predict 'cow', but MMCL successfully learns the cow; (2) the inter-class feature sharing enabled by the MMCL loss allows learning information about a class that only exists and is annotated in other classes. For example, if all the images of the tree class have green leaves but an image in the wolf class has a tree without leaves in its background, MMCL can disassociate the green leaf from the tree class. SL, in contrast, cannot leverage this information and learns the green leaves as an indistinguishable part of 'tree', so it fails to classify trees without green leaves in the test data. Together, both mechanisms enable MMCL to learn representations that are robust against distribution shift and generalize to unseen domains.

Furthermore, to emphasize the importance of captions, we analyze the effect of varying caption richness and show that rich captions are essential for achieving robustness. In the extreme case where the captions are merely labels, no gains in robustness can be achieved.

We further support our theoretical findings with experiments, including a well-designed synthetic experiment and experiments on real datasets such as MSCOCO, Conceptual Captions, and shifted versions of ImageNet. The results demonstrate the crucial roles of the MMCL loss function and rich captions in achieving robustness, further validating our theoretical findings.

References:
